explanations.answer: A gentle lamb led to slaughter
explanations.explanation: That's the picture, friend. Jeremiah, the prophet, says, “…I was like a gentle lamb led to slaughter…” A lamb just trotting along, no clue what's coming. I think that's a tender thing to say about yourself.

A watchman sounds like somebody who sees trouble coming. Jeremiah's picture is the other way around. He says he was like a gentle lamb led to slaughter, and that he did not know about the plot. Honestly, I'd make a terrible watchman anyway, I nod off standing up on my gold base.
Soldier is a tough picture, and Jeremiah went much softer. He says he was like a gentle lamb led to slaughter. A lamb doesn't pack a bag for battle. I think he's telling us he never saw this coming.

Right, and he says it plainly: “I did not know that they had plotted against me…” He was walking around with no idea. Then the LORD informed him, so he knew. Finding out what people have planned behind your back is a heavy thing.

The text says the opposite. Jeremiah says, “I did not know that they had plotted against me…” That was before the LORD informed him, and then he knew. So he starts out in the dark and then gets let in on it.
Not quite, friend. Jeremiah hands it over instead. He says, “…for to You I have committed my cause.” He asks to see the LORD's vengeance, and he never says he'll take care of the plotters himself.

Yes, that's the catch. Jeremiah says to the LORD, “…for to You I have committed my cause.” He's putting it in the LORD's hands. He asks to see the LORD's vengeance, and he never says he'll take care of the plotters himself.

That's the word he uses. He says, “…let me see Your vengeance upon them…” He's talking to the LORD of Hosts, who judges righteously and examines the heart and mind. And remember, he's committed his cause to Him.
Mercy is a good word, but it's not the one Jeremiah says here. He asks the LORD of Hosts to let him see His vengeance upon them. The text puts the request in his mouth just like that.

Glory is a big word, and Jeremiah doesn't use it in this spot. He says, “…let me see Your vengeance upon them…” It's all there in verse 20, right after he calls the LORD of Hosts the One who examines the heart and mind.

explanations.answer: Prophesy in the name of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it. The people of Anathoth say, “You must not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand.” They're seeking his life over it. I think that's one of the hardest things a person could hear, especially from his own hometown (Jeremiah 1:1).
The text doesn't mention sacrifices here. The people of Anathoth tell him, “You must not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand.” His prophesying is what they're after.
Nobody says a word about leaving town. What they say is, “You must not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand.” The warning is about his words from the LORD.
Yes. The LORD of Hosts says it Himself: “I will punish them.” Then He says what that will look like. Notice He's answering the people who were seeking Jeremiah's life.
No second warning shows up in these verses. The LORD of Hosts says, “I will punish them.” He goes right on to describe the punishment, the sword and famine.
Forgiveness isn't what He says here. The LORD of Hosts says, “I will punish them.” Then He talks about the sword for their young men and famine for their sons and daughters.
The text says the opposite, friend. The LORD says, “There will be no remnant…” That means nobody is left over. It's a heavy word, and I think it's fair to say so.
Right. The LORD says, “There will be no remnant…” He'll bring disaster on the people of Anathoth in the year of their punishment. It's a heavy line, so I'll just let it sit there.

That's the question Jeremiah brings: “Why does the way of the wicked prosper?” He even says he wishes to contend with the LORD about His judgments. And he starts by saying, “Righteous are You, O LORD…” I like that he talks straight to the LORD.
Humble isn't the word. Jeremiah asks, “Why does the way of the wicked prosper?” It's the wicked who seem to be doing well, and that's what's bugging him. He brings it right to the LORD.
Poor doesn't show up in his question. He asks, “Why does the way of the wicked prosper?” He adds, “Why do all the faithless live at ease?” That's the puzzle he's laying out before the LORD.
Careful, friend, it's the other way around. Jeremiah says, “You are ever on their lips, but far from their hearts.” They talk about the LORD all the time. It's their hearts that are far away.
Yes. Jeremiah says, “You are ever on their lips, but far from their hearts.” So the LORD's name is always in their mouths. Their hearts are somewhere else.
That's what he says. “You are ever on their lips, but far from their hearts.” The words say one thing and the hearts say another. Nice talk and a far away heart don't match.
Fear isn't in the text. Jeremiah says the LORD is “…ever on their lips, but far from their hearts.” The hearts are far away, and that's the whole point.
The text doesn't say anything about them changing. Jeremiah says, “You are ever on their lips, but far from their hearts.” He describes the way things stand, with the hearts far away.

explanations.answer: Haul them off like sheep for slaughter
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jeremiah says, “Drag away the wicked like sheep to the slaughter…” He also asks the LORD to set them apart for the day of carnage. He says this right after saying the LORD knows him, sees him and tests his heart toward Him.

explanations.answer: Let them wander off like lost sheep
explanations.explanation: Wandering off sounds almost gentle, and that's not what he asks. He says, “Drag away the wicked like sheep to the slaughter…” It's a firm request. He follows it with a request to set them apart for the day of carnage.

explanations.answer: Give them one more year to change
explanations.explanation: There's no extra year in his request. Jeremiah says, “Drag away the wicked like sheep to the slaughter…” That's what he asks the LORD to do with them.

That's what he says. “Because of the evil of its residents, the animals and birds have been swept away…” He also asks how long the land will mourn and the grass of every field be withered. The whole land is feeling it.

The text says it is true. Jeremiah says, “Because of the evil of its residents, the animals and birds have been swept away…” He asks how long the land will mourn, with the grass of every field withered. The whole land is hurting.

Yes, horses. The words say, “…how can you compete with horses?” If men on foot already wore you out, horses are a whole other level. It's like getting winded on the walk to the mailbox and then signing up for a marathon. Bold move, friend.

Camels didn't make it into this picture. The words ask, “…how can you compete with horses?” It goes from men on foot straight to horses. Camels never even got a turn at the starting line, poor things.
No lions here, friend. The race picture says, “…how can you compete with horses?” It goes from men on foot to horses. Nobody's getting chased by a lion in this one, and honestly, my hat is relieved.
Yes, brothers. The words say, “…even they have betrayed you…” and they point to his own father's household. That one stings. It's the same kind of hurt we saw earlier with the people of Anathoth.
Soldiers aren't named here. The words point to your brothers, your own father's household, and say, “…even they have betrayed you…” This one's about family.
Rulers don't come up in this line. The words say your brothers, your own father's household, “…even they have betrayed you…” This one's about family.
Careful, friend, it says the opposite. The words say, “Do not trust them, though they speak well of you.” Nice words from them don't change that. It's a hard thing to hear about your own family.
Yes. The words say, “Do not trust them, though they speak well of you.” So even kind talk from his father's household isn't a reason to trust them. I think that's a lonely place for Jeremiah to be.
